title: Privacy Spotter
instruction: Routine data use, or a privacy risk?

items.text: The app remembers the language you picked
items.why: A setting you chose, stored to serve you. Nothing about you is inferred.

items.text: A login cookie keeps you signed in
items.why: First-party and functional: needed for the service you asked for.

items.text: A shop recommends accessories based on what you bought in that same shop
items.why: First-party data used inside the service that collected it: the normal job of a recommender.

items.text: Your watch history is kept so you can resume, and you can delete it
items.why: Useful, first-party, and under your control: the delete button keeps it routine.

items.text: Your dark-mode preference is saved on your device
items.why: A local display setting that reveals nothing about you.

items.text: A tracker follows you across unrelated websites
items.why: Cross-site tracking is AdTech, not the platform's recommender: a company you never dealt with builds a profile of you.

items.text: Your browsing profile is sold to a data broker
items.why: Your data leaves the service you chose, for purposes you never saw.

items.text: Your precise location is recorded around the clock, even when the app is closed
items.why: Far beyond what the service needs, and location trails can identify a person on their own.

items.text: The app infers your health condition from what you browse
items.why: A sensitive trait you never shared: the model of your behaviour knows more than you told it.

items.text: Your viewing history is shared with advertisers
items.why: Viewing history reveals interests and beliefs. Sharing it outside the platform is the risk.

debrief: Platforms build a digital twin of you: a model of your behaviour, built from interaction data, that needs no name to work. The line is not whether data is collected, but whether it stays in the service you chose and whether you can see and control it.
